title: Hash maps & complements
summary: A hash map remembers information so you do not have to search for it again. Lookups take expected constant time.
intuition: Keep a notebook of values already seen. Before writing down the current value, check whether its partner is in the notebook.
clues: Pair sums, duplicate detection, counting, or repeated membership checks. Hash keys must represent exactly the property you need.
example: At index 0, partner 7 is missing. Store 2 → 0.
At index 1, partner 2 is present. Return [0, 1].
state: seen maps a previously visited value to its index.
invariant: Every stored index is earlier than the current one, so a value cannot pair with itself.
time: O(n) expected: one pass with expected O(1) lookups.
pitfalls: Inserting before checking can reuse the same index. Hash operations are expected O(1), not guaranteed worst-case O(1).
edges: Duplicate values such as [3,3]; no pair; negative values.
brute: Check every pair in O(n²) time and O(1) space. Sorting permits two pointers but requires keeping original indices.
interview: I would keep a notebook of values already seen. Before writing down the current value, check whether its partner is in the notebook. The key guarantee is: Every stored index is earlier than the current one, so a value cannot pair with itself.
followup: Why check before inserting?
simpler: Keep a notebook of values already seen. Before writing down the current value, check whether its partner is in the notebook.

quiz.question: Why check before inserting?
options: To avoid reusing the same index
quiz.explanation: The map contains only earlier indices, which guarantees two distinct positions.

title: Two pointers
summary: Two pointers inspect two positions and move them using a rule that safely eliminates candidates. Sorted input often provides this rule.
intuition: Start at both ends of a sorted array. If the sum is too small, move the smaller end; if it is too big, move the larger end.
clues: Sorted pair sums, palindromes, partitioning, and merging sorted sequences. The safe movement rule changes by problem.
example: For target 8: 1 + 8 is too big, then 1 + 5 too small, then 3 + 5 succeeds.
state: left, right, and their current sum.
invariant: When the sum is too small, the left value cannot pair with any value at or before right. The symmetric argument removes right when too large.
time: O(n): each pointer only moves inward.
pitfalls: Applying this sum rule to unsorted data discards valid pairs. Sorting can lose original indices.
edges: Empty array, one item, duplicates, no solution.
brute: All pairs cost O(n²). Hashing works without sorting using O(n) space.
interview: I would start at both ends of a sorted array. If the sum is too small, move the smaller end; if it is too big, move the larger end. The key guarantee is: When the sum is too small, the left value cannot pair with any value at or before right. The symmetric argument removes right when too large.
followup: Would this movement rule work on [8,1,5,3]?
simpler: Start at both ends of a sorted array. If the sum is too small, move the smaller end; if it is too big, move the larger end.

quiz.question: Would this movement rule work on [8,1,5,3]?
options: Only if the target is positive
quiz.explanation: On unsorted input a smaller index does not imply a smaller value.

title: Sliding window
summary: Maintain a contiguous section instead of repeatedly scanning substrings. Expand to include the next item, then shrink until the exact validity rule holds.
intuition: Imagine a frame over a string. Widen it one character at a time; if a character repeats, move the left edge until all characters inside are distinct.
clues: Contiguous ranges with a condition that can be repaired by removing leftmost items. Not every range condition supports this.
example: Read a, b, c: window "abc", best = 3.
Next a repeats. Remove the first a, leaving "bc", then add a.
state: left, right, a set of characters in the current window, and best length.
invariant: After shrinking and adding the current character, the window contains each character at most once. All later left boundaries produce no longer window.
time: O(n) expected: each character enters and leaves at most once.
space: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the set.
pitfalls: Use while, not if: removing one character may not remove the duplicate. Sum windows with negatives lack the usual monotonicity.
edges: Empty string, all identical characters, Unicode, duplicate far from left.
brute: Enumerate every start and expand until a duplicate: O(n²) worst-case.
interview: I would imagine a frame over a string. Widen it one character at a time; if a character repeats, move the left edge until all characters inside are distinct. The key guarantee is: After shrinking and adding the current character, the window contains each character at most once. All later left boundaries produce no longer window.
followup: After reading the last b in "abba", how far must left move?
simpler: Imagine a frame over a string. Widen it one character at a time; if a character repeats, move the left edge until all characters inside are distinct.

quiz.question: After reading the last b in "abba", how far must left move?
options: Until the previous b is removed
quiz.explanation: Removing a alone still leaves two b characters. Continue until the previous b leaves.

title: Character replacement: stale max frequency
summary: For a window of length w, w minus its largest character count is the number of replacements needed. A historical maximum frequency can find the best length without maintaining an always-valid current window.
intuition: Keep the strongest repetition count ever seen. A later window may be invalid, but it cannot beat the previously justified length unless that record count increases.
clues: Longest equal-character substring after at most k replacements. This historical-count shortcut is specific to maximizing length.
example: Window AABA has maxfreq 3 and length 4: one replacement.
Later counts can fall while maxfreq stays 3. Length 4 is already justified.
Growing beyond 4 requires a new higher maxfreq; stale counts cannot invent a larger valid answer.
state: counts, left, historical maxfreq, and best.
invariant: The maintained length never grows beyond maxfreq + k. A record maxfreq is witnessed in a real window; when best grows, that witness justifies the new best length.
time: O(n) expected because each pointer moves at most n times.
pitfalls: Do not claim every current window is valid with a stale maxfreq. Returning its endpoints needs extra care; this template returns only a length.
edges: k = 0, empty input, k larger than string length.
brute: Recompute the current maximum after shrinking for an easier invariant; with 26 letters this is still O(26n).
interview: I would keep the strongest repetition count ever seen. A later window may be invalid, but it cannot beat the previously justified length unless that record count increases. The key guarantee is: The maintained length never grows beyond maxfreq + k. A record maxfreq is witnessed in a real window; when best grows, that witness justifies the new best length.
followup: Does stale maxfreq guarantee the current window is valid?
simpler: Keep the strongest repetition count ever seen. A later window may be invalid, but it cannot beat the previously justified length unless that record count increases.

quiz.question: Does stale maxfreq guarantee the current window is valid?
options: No; it preserves the best-length computation
quiz.explanation: A stale count can overestimate current frequency. The result relies on a previously witnessed length, not universal window validity.

title: Prefix sums
summary: A prefix sum stores the total before each position. Subtract two prefix values to answer a range sum without scanning it.
intuition: Keep a running odometer. The distance traveled between two stops is the later reading minus the earlier reading.
clues: Many static range sums, subarray sum equals k with negative values, or preprocessing before queries.
example: Sum of half-open range [1, 3) = prefix[3] - prefix[1] = 3.
state: prefix[i] is the sum of nums[:i].
invariant: prefix[right] includes everything before right; subtracting prefix[left] removes everything before left.
time: O(n) preprocessing; O(1) per query after building prefix once.
pitfalls: Mixing inclusive and exclusive indices. Rebuilding prefix per query loses the preprocessing benefit.
edges: Empty range; full range; negative numbers; zero values.
brute: Each direct range sum takes O(range length). For frequent updates consider a Fenwick tree.
interview: I would keep a running odometer. The distance traveled between two stops is the later reading minus the earlier reading. The key guarantee is: prefix[right] includes everything before right; subtracting prefix[left] removes everything before left.
followup: Why can prefix sums handle negative numbers?
simpler: Keep a running odometer. The distance traveled between two stops is the later reading minus the earlier reading.

quiz.question: Why can prefix sums handle negative numbers?
options: Subtraction is algebraic and does not require monotonicity
quiz.explanation: The cancellation identity holds regardless of the signs of the numbers.

title: Binary search
summary: Binary search discards half of a sorted search space at each step. Define whether the endpoints are included before choosing updates.
intuition: Check the middle of a sorted shelf. If the target is larger, every item to the left of that middle is too small.
clues: Sorted data or a monotonic predicate. Exact lookup and boundary search use different invariants.
example: left = 0, right = 4, mid = 2: value 5 is too small.
state: Inclusive left and right; mid = left + (right-left)//2.
invariant: If the target exists, it remains in nums[left:right+1]. Every unsuccessful iteration removes mid and at least half of the candidates.
time: O(log n) comparisons as the candidate count halves.
pitfalls: Updating left = mid in this inclusive template may never terminate. A boundary search uses a different contract.
edges: Empty input, one value, absent target, duplicates.
brute: Linear scan is O(n), useful when data is unsorted and there is only one query.
interview: I would check the middle of a sorted shelf. If the target is larger, every item to the left of that middle is too small. The key guarantee is: If the target exists, it remains in nums[left:right+1]. Every unsuccessful iteration removes mid and at least half of the candidates.
followup: Why use left <= right for exact lookup?
simpler: Check the middle of a sorted shelf. If the target is larger, every item to the left of that middle is too small.

quiz.question: Why use left <= right for exact lookup?
options: To examine a final single candidate
Because every binary search requires it
quiz.explanation: When left equals right, one untested candidate remains in an inclusive interval.

title: Binary search on the answer
summary: Search possible answers when you can efficiently check feasibility and feasibility changes in only one direction.
intuition: Try a work speed. If it finishes in time, all faster speeds also work, so look for the slowest feasible speed.
clues: Minimize a maximum, capacity, speed, or threshold with a monotonic feasibility test. Prove monotonicity first.
example: Speed 4 needs 8 hours: minimum feasible speed.
state: left and right bound the first feasible speed; hours is the sum of ceiling divisions.
invariant: The minimum feasible speed stays in [left, right]. A feasible mid stays as right because it could be the answer.
time: O(n log M), with M = maximum pile: each check scans n piles.
pitfalls: Using floor instead of ceiling division. Assuming feasibility when h is smaller than the number of positive piles.
edges: Positive piles; h equal to pile count; no feasible speed; empty piles.
brute: Try all speeds 1 through M in O(nM).
interview: I would try a work speed. If it finishes in time, all faster speeds also work, so look for the slowest feasible speed. The key guarantee is: The minimum feasible speed stays in [left, right]. A feasible mid stays as right because it could be the answer.
followup: If mid works, why retain it as right?
simpler: Try a work speed. If it finishes in time, all faster speeds also work, so look for the slowest feasible speed.

quiz.question: If mid works, why retain it as right?
options: It may be the minimum feasible answer
quiz.explanation: Discarding a feasible mid could discard the first feasible speed.

title: Linked list reversal
summary: Reverse a list by redirecting each next pointer toward the already-reversed prefix. Save the original next node before changing any link.
intuition: Turn each arrow around while keeping a bookmark for where to go next.
clues: In-place list transformations, reversed halves, palindrome checking, and reordering.
example: Save 2; point 1 to None. prev = 1, current = 2.
Save 3; point 2 to 1. Then point 3 to 2.
state: prev, current, and following.
invariant: prev is the reversed processed prefix; current begins the unchanged remaining suffix.
time: Reversal is O(n); each node is visited once.
space: Reversal uses O(1); the list-conversion test wrapper uses O(n).
pitfalls: Losing the suffix by overwriting current.next too early. Returning current instead of prev.
edges: Empty list, singleton, cyclic input is outside this template contract.
brute: A stack can reverse values in O(n) extra space, but does not teach in-place pointer reversal.
interview: I would turn each arrow around while keeping a bookmark for where to go next. The key guarantee is: prev is the reversed processed prefix; current begins the unchanged remaining suffix.
followup: Which pointer must be saved before redirecting current.next?
simpler: Turn each arrow around while keeping a bookmark for where to go next.

quiz.question: Which pointer must be saved before redirecting current.next?
quiz.explanation: The saved successor is the only path to the unprocessed suffix.

title: Tree DFS & return values
summary: Recursive tree algorithms ask each child for a specific piece of information. For height, each child returns its height and the parent adds one to the larger value.
intuition: Ask each branch how tall it is. A parent only needs those two answers to describe its own height.
clues: Subtree aggregates, depth, balance, diameter, and lowest common ancestors. Define the return value before writing recursion.
state: A call stack and the height returned by each child. Here a node is [value, left, right].
invariant: Each call returns the correct height of its own subtree because it combines correct child heights with one level for itself.
time: O(n): one visit per node.
space: O(h) call stack, O(n) for a skewed tree.
pitfalls: Mixing edge-count and node-count heights. Recomputing subtree heights repeatedly can make balance checks O(n²).
edges: Empty root; skewed tree; single leaf. Python recursion can overflow for deep trees.
brute: BFS counts levels using O(width) space. Iterative DFS avoids the interpreter recursion limit.
interview: I would ask each branch how tall it is. A parent only needs those two answers to describe its own height. The key guarantee is: Each call returns the correct height of its own subtree because it combines correct child heights with one level for itself.
followup: What is the height of an empty tree in this node-count convention?
simpler: Ask each branch how tall it is. A parent only needs those two answers to describe its own height.

quiz.question: What is the height of an empty tree in this node-count convention?
quiz.explanation: An empty tree contributes zero nodes to a root-to-leaf path.

title: Tries & shared prefixes
summary: A trie stores characters along paths so words sharing a prefix share nodes. A terminal marker distinguishes complete words from prefixes.
intuition: Build a branching signpost: follow one character per turn, then check whether the path ends at a real word.
clues: Prefix queries, autocomplete, word dictionaries, and grid word search with prefix pruning.
example: Both share c → a; then branch to t or r.
Search ca reaches a path but no terminal marker, so it is not a full word.
state: A dictionary per node and a terminal marker.
invariant: The path from the root spells exactly the prefix represented by that node.
time: O(total inserted characters + query length) expected.
space: O(total inserted characters) nodes in the worst case.
pitfalls: Treating an existing path as a complete word. Deleting shared nodes without checking other words.
edges: Empty word, one word being a prefix of another, repeated inserts.
brute: A hash set is simpler for exact membership only. Tries help when prefix structure matters.
interview: I would build a branching signpost: follow one character per turn, then check whether the path ends at a real word. The key guarantee is: The path from the root spells exactly the prefix represented by that node.
followup: After inserting "care", is "car" necessarily a word?
simpler: Build a branching signpost: follow one character per turn, then check whether the path ends at a real word.

quiz.question: After inserting "care", is "car" necessarily a word?
options: No, it needs its own terminal marker
Only if the trie is sorted
quiz.explanation: Path existence proves a prefix exists; a terminal marker proves a complete word exists.

title: Heaps & top k
summary: A min heap makes the smallest item available at the root. Push and pop restore this partial ordering in logarithmic time.
intuition: Keep only the k strongest candidates. The weakest candidate sits at the door, ready to leave when a stronger one arrives.
clues: Repeated minimum extraction, top k, streaming rankings, and merging sorted streams. Sorting once may be simpler for static data.
example: Reading 2 pushes out 2. Heap contains 3 and 5.
The root 3 is the second largest.
state: A min heap containing at most k values.
invariant: After each item, the heap contains the k largest values seen so far, or all values if fewer than k have been seen.
time: O(n log k); for k=1 this is O(n).
pitfalls: Assuming the entire heap array is sorted. Python tuple heap entries compare later fields on ties.
edges: k = 1; k = n; duplicates count as separate items; invalid k.
brute: Sort in O(n log n), or use quickselect for expected O(n) with a worst-case O(n²) caveat.
interview: I would keep only the k strongest candidates. The weakest candidate sits at the door, ready to leave when a stronger one arrives. The key guarantee is: After each item, the heap contains the k largest values seen so far, or all values if fewer than k have been seen.
followup: Why use a min heap to keep the k largest values?
simpler: Keep only the k strongest candidates. The weakest candidate sits at the door, ready to leave when a stronger one arrives.

quiz.question: Why use a min heap to keep the k largest values?
options: To remove the smallest retained candidate
Because the whole heap is descending
quiz.explanation: The root exposes the weakest of the retained largest values.

title: Monotonic stacks
summary: A monotonic stack keeps candidates in increasing or decreasing order. A new value resolves and removes earlier candidates that it dominates.
intuition: Keep a waiting line of unresolved days. A warmer day answers every colder day at the end of the line.
clues: Next greater/smaller element, daily temperatures, histogram boundaries. Store indices when distance matters.
example: Day 3 resolves day 2: wait 1, then day 1: wait 2.
state: Stack of indices whose temperatures are nonincreasing; answer distances.
invariant: Unresolved days stay on the stack. When a day is popped, the current day is its first strictly warmer successor.
time: O(n): each index is pushed and popped at most once.
pitfalls: Popping on equality when the question asks for strictly warmer. Storing values loses distance information.
edges: Equal temperatures; descending sequence; empty input.
brute: Scan rightward from each day in O(n²).
interview: I would keep a waiting line of unresolved days. A warmer day answers every colder day at the end of the line. The key guarantee is: Unresolved days stay on the stack. When a day is popped, the current day is its first strictly warmer successor.
followup: What does the nested while loop do to total complexity?
simpler: Keep a waiting line of unresolved days. A warmer day answers every colder day at the end of the line.

quiz.question: What does the nested while loop do to total complexity?
options: Still O(n), since each index is popped once
quiz.explanation: Amortized analysis counts total pushes and pops across the whole input.

title: Backtracking
summary: Backtracking explores a decision tree, then restores state before trying another branch. Pruning skips branches that cannot produce an answer.
intuition: Choose an item, explore everything possible with that choice, then put it back before trying the next choice.
clues: Generate subsets, permutations, combinations, or assignments under constraints. Output size may already be exponential.
example: Choose 2 and record [1,2], then undo 2 and undo 1.
Choose 2 from the root and record [2].
state: path, the next allowed index, and a result list.
invariant: path contains exactly the choices on the current branch. Starting later indices avoids generating the same index subset twice.
time: O(n · 2^n) including copying all output subsets.
pitfalls: Appending path without copying. Forgetting pop. Duplicate input values require additional duplicate handling.
edges: Empty input produces [[]]; distinct input assumed; large output.
brute: Bit masks can enumerate the same subsets. Memoization is useful for repeated states, not automatically for listing distinct paths.
interview: I would choose an item, explore everything possible with that choice, then put it back before trying the next choice. The key guarantee is: path contains exactly the choices on the current branch. Starting later indices avoids generating the same index subset twice.
followup: Why copy path when storing a result?
simpler: Choose an item, explore everything possible with that choice, then put it back before trying the next choice.

quiz.question: Why copy path when storing a result?
options: Because later mutations would change stored references
quiz.explanation: Every branch reuses and mutates path; each answer must keep its own snapshot.

title: Breadth-first search
summary: BFS visits vertices in increasing number of edges from a source. A FIFO queue preserves this layer order.
intuition: Spread a wave one edge per round. The first wave to reach a vertex used the fewest edges.
clues: Unweighted shortest paths, level order, nearest sources, and grid distance where every move has equal cost.
state: Adjacency list, queue, and distances (which also mark visited nodes).
invariant: Vertices leave the queue in nondecreasing distance. First discovery assigns the shortest edge-count path.
time: O(V + E), examining each reachable vertex and adjacency entry once.
space: O(V) for distances and queue, excluding the graph.
pitfalls: Marking visited on pop can enqueue duplicates. BFS does not minimize arbitrary weighted cost.
edges: Disconnected nodes remain -1; cycles; self-loops; source must be a valid index.
brute: DFS finds reachability but not necessarily the shortest route. Dijkstra handles nonnegative weights.
interview: I would spread a wave one edge per round. The first wave to reach a vertex used the fewest edges. The key guarantee is: Vertices leave the queue in nondecreasing distance. First discovery assigns the shortest edge-count path.
followup: Does ordinary BFS minimize cost when edges cost 1 or 10?
simpler: Spread a wave one edge per round. The first wave to reach a vertex used the fewest edges.

quiz.question: Does ordinary BFS minimize cost when edges cost 1 or 10?
options: No, layer order counts edges rather than cost
quiz.explanation: A one-edge route costing 10 can be worse than two edges costing 1 each.

title: Topological sorting
summary: A topological order places prerequisites before dependents in a directed acyclic graph. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with no remaining prerequisites.
intuition: Schedule whichever tasks are ready. Finishing a task may unlock others. If unfinished tasks remain and none are ready, there is a cycle.
clues: Dependency ordering, courses, build systems, and DAG dynamic programming. Edges point from prerequisite to dependent.
state: Indegrees, a queue of zero-indegree vertices, and output order.
invariant: A ready vertex has no unfinished prerequisite, so placing it next never violates an edge.
code:
from collections import deque

def solve(n, edges):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        graph[a].append(b)
        indegree[b] += 1
    ready = deque(i for i in range(n) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while ready:
        node = ready.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            indegree[neighbor] -= 1
            if indegree[neighbor] == 0:
                ready.append(neighbor)
    return order if len(order) == n else []
time: O(V + E): count each edge, then remove it once.
pitfalls: Reversing prerequisite edges. Returning a partial order as if it solved a cyclic graph.
edges: Disconnected tasks, no edges, self-cycle, multiple valid orders.
brute: DFS postorder with three-color cycle detection also gives a topological order.
interview: I would schedule whichever tasks are ready. Finishing a task may unlock others. If unfinished tasks remain and none are ready, there is a cycle. The key guarantee is: A ready vertex has no unfinished prerequisite, so placing it next never violates an edge.
followup: What does processing fewer than n vertices indicate?
simpler: Schedule whichever tasks are ready. Finishing a task may unlock others. If unfinished tasks remain and none are ready, there is a cycle.

quiz.question: What does processing fewer than n vertices indicate?
options: At least one directed cycle blocks completion
quiz.explanation: Disconnected DAG vertices still become ready. A directed cycle cannot remove its final incoming prerequisites.

title: Union-Find
summary: Union-Find maintains disjoint components under merges. Each component has a representative root; path compression and union by size keep operations fast.
intuition: Give each group a leader. Joining groups changes one leader pointer, and looking up a leader shortens the route for next time.
clues: Incremental undirected connectivity, redundant edges, and Kruskal’s minimum spanning tree. It does not return actual paths.
example: First two edges leave two components.
The third joins their different roots, leaving one component.
state: parent, component sizes, and number of components.
invariant: Every parent chain ends at the representative of exactly one component. Joining distinct roots merges exactly two components.
time: O((V + E) α(V)) amortized; α grows extraordinarily slowly.
pitfalls: Joining arbitrary nodes rather than roots. Using ordinary Union-Find for deletions or directed reachability.
edges: Repeated edges, isolated vertices, self-loops, n = 0.
brute: One DFS/BFS computes static components in O(V + E); Union-Find is helpful for incremental merges.
interview: I would give each group a leader. Joining groups changes one leader pointer, and looking up a leader shortens the route for next time. The key guarantee is: Every parent chain ends at the representative of exactly one component. Joining distinct roots merges exactly two components.
followup: Can this structure directly return the shortest path?
simpler: Give each group a leader. Joining groups changes one leader pointer, and looking up a leader shortens the route for next time.

quiz.question: Can this structure directly return the shortest path?
options: No, it stores components rather than graph paths
Only if union by size is used
quiz.explanation: Parent pointers describe component membership, not original graph edges.

title: Dijkstra’s shortest paths
summary: Dijkstra repeatedly expands the unsettled vertex with smallest known distance. Nonnegative weights make that distance final.
intuition: Always extend the cheapest unfinished route. With no negative edges, a more expensive route cannot come back and improve the cheapest one.
clues: Shortest paths with nonnegative edge weights. Use BFS for equal weights, 0–1 BFS for weights 0/1, and Bellman–Ford when negatives matter.
example: Pop (3,1). Later (4,1) is stale and skipped.
state: Min heap of (distance, vertex), distance array, weighted adjacency list.
invariant: A non-stale minimum popped distance cannot be improved through an unsettled vertex when all edges are nonnegative.
time: O((V + E) log(E + 1)) with lazy heap entries; commonly O((V + E) log V) on simple graphs.
space: O(V + E) including stale heap entries, excluding input.
pitfalls: Negative weights invalidate the finalization proof. Marking visited when pushing can lock in a bad distance.
edges: Zero-weight edges, unreachable nodes (None here), duplicate edges, source only.
brute: Bellman–Ford is O(VE) and supports negative edges with negative-cycle detection.
interview: I would always extend the cheapest unfinished route. With no negative edges, a more expensive route cannot come back and improve the cheapest one. The key guarantee is: A non-stale minimum popped distance cannot be improved through an unsettled vertex when all edges are nonnegative.
followup: Why skip an entry whose cost differs from distance[node]?
simpler: Always extend the cheapest unfinished route. With no negative edges, a more expensive route cannot come back and improve the cheapest one.

quiz.question: Why skip an entry whose cost differs from distance[node]?
options: It is an outdated route already improved
quiz.explanation: Relaxation inserted a better entry. Expanding the old one repeats unnecessary work.

title: Edge-limited relaxation
summary: For a path with at most k stops, allow at most k + 1 edges. Relax all edges from the previous round’s distances to enforce this budget.
intuition: Give every route one extra ticket per round. Read from yesterday’s notebook and write into a fresh copy, so a new route cannot spend several tickets in one round.
clues: Cheapest flights with stop limits, bounded path length, and Bellman–Ford style dynamic programming.
example: One edge is allowed. Snapshot starts [0,∞,∞].
For k = 1, the next round reaches 2 for cost 2.
state: distances from paths using at most r edges; a copied next-distance array.
invariant: After r rounds, each distance is the cheapest cost using at most r edges. Reading only the old array prevents accidental extra edges.
time: O((k + 1)(V + E)) here, including V-element copies each round.
pitfalls: Updating in place can traverse multiple edges in one round. k stops means k+1 edges. This bounded variant does not detect unbounded negative cycles.
edges: Direct-only route, unreachable target, source equals target, edge order changes.
brute: Ordinary Bellman–Ford uses V−1 rounds and an extra pass to detect reachable negative cycles. Dijkstra with only one distance per node does not encode a stop budget.
interview: I would give every route one extra ticket per round. Read from yesterday’s notebook and write into a fresh copy, so a new route cannot spend several tickets in one round. The key guarantee is: After r rounds, each distance is the cheapest cost using at most r edges. Reading only the old array prevents accidental extra edges.
followup: Why use a snapshot for each round?
simpler: Give every route one extra ticket per round. Read from yesterday’s notebook and write into a fresh copy, so a new route cannot spend several tickets in one round.

quiz.question: Why use a snapshot for each round?
options: To restrict paths to one additional edge
quiz.explanation: Reading a newly updated distance could chain multiple edges inside the same round.

title: Dynamic programming: state first
summary: Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once. Define the meaning of a state, its base case, and which smaller states it depends on.
intuition: For each amount, write down the fewest coins needed. To make amount a, try taking one coin c after an optimal solution for a−c.
clues: Minimum/maximum/counting problems with reusable subproblems and a state that captures everything affecting future choices.
state: dp[a] = minimum coin count for amount a; infinity means unreachable.
invariant: When computing a, every dp[a−c] is already optimal because positive c makes a−c smaller. Trying every final coin covers every solution.
time: O(amount × number of coins): one transition per usable coin per state.
pitfalls: Greedy fails for arbitrary denominations. Zero/negative coins break this recurrence’s dependency order; require positive coins and nonnegative amount.
edges: Amount 0, impossible amount, no coins, denominations larger than amount.
brute: Uncached recursion repeats subproblems exponentially. Memoization reaches the same states on demand.
interview: I would for each amount, write down the fewest coins needed. To make amount a, try taking one coin c after an optimal solution for a−c. The key guarantee is: When computing a, every dp[a−c] is already optimal because positive c makes a−c smaller. Trying every final coin covers every solution.
followup: For coins [1,3,4] and amount 6, why does largest-first fail?
simpler: For each amount, write down the fewest coins needed. To make amount a, try taking one coin c after an optimal solution for a−c.

quiz.question: For coins [1,3,4] and amount 6, why does largest-first fail?
quiz.explanation: A locally large coin is not always part of a globally minimum-count solution.

title: 2-D DP: longest common subsequence
summary: Use two indices when progress in two sequences determines the remaining problem. A subsequence keeps order but may skip elements.
intuition: Compare the first remaining character of each string. If they match, keep one shared character; otherwise try skipping from either string.
clues: Sequence alignment, edit distance, matching subsequences, and two independent positions.
example: Last row and column represent an empty suffix: all zero.
Matching e contributes 1. Matching c contributes 1 plus the e answer.
Matching a contributes 1 plus the ce answer: 3.
state: dp[i][j] = LCS length of a[i:] and b[j:]. Evaluate from bottom-right to top-left.
invariant: A match allows 1 + dp[i+1][j+1]. Without a match, at least one first character must be skipped, so take the best of the two possibilities.
time: O(mn): m × n states, constant work per state.
space: O(mn). Two-row optimization reduces this to O(min(m,n)) if only the length is needed.
pitfalls: Confusing substring with subsequence. Using [[0]*n]*m shares row objects. Filling before dependencies are ready.
edges: Empty string, no matches, repeated letters, identical strings.
brute: Enumerating subsequences is exponential. Top-down memoization uses the same state with a recursion stack.
interview: I would compare the first remaining character of each string. If they match, keep one shared character; otherwise try skipping from either string. The key guarantee is: A match allows 1 + dp[i+1][j+1]. Without a match, at least one first character must be skipped, so take the best of the two possibilities.
followup: Why fill from bottom-right?
simpler: Compare the first remaining character of each string. If they match, keep one shared character; otherwise try skipping from either string.

quiz.question: Why fill from bottom-right?
options: The answer is always at the bottom
quiz.explanation: dp[i+1][j] and dp[i][j+1] must already be computed.

title: Greedy & exchange arguments
summary: A greedy algorithm commits to a local choice only when you can prove it preserves an optimal solution. For maximum nonoverlapping meetings, choose the earliest finishing meeting.
intuition: Finish the next meeting as early as possible to leave the most room for everything that follows.
clues: Scheduling when a dominance or exchange argument exists. An appealing local rule alone is not a proof.
state: Sorted intervals, finish time of the last selected meeting, and selected count.
invariant: Replace the first meeting of an optimal schedule with the earliest-finishing one: it ends no later and cannot block later meetings. Repeat on the remaining suffix.
time: O(n log n) for sorting, then O(n) scanning.
space: O(n) for sorted copy (Python sorting also uses auxiliary storage).
pitfalls: Choosing earliest start can select one long meeting and block many short ones. Weighted meetings require a different strategy, often DP.
edges: Touching endpoints are allowed here; empty set; negative times.
brute: Enumerate subsets for exponential time, or DP for weighted interval scheduling.
interview: I would finish the next meeting as early as possible to leave the most room for everything that follows. The key guarantee is: Replace the first meeting of an optimal schedule with the earliest-finishing one: it ends no later and cannot block later meetings. Repeat on the remaining suffix.
followup: Does earliest finish solve maximum-value meetings with unequal values?
simpler: Finish the next meeting as early as possible to leave the most room for everything that follows.

quiz.question: Does earliest finish solve maximum-value meetings with unequal values?
options: No, the exchange proof ignores value
quiz.explanation: One high-value long interval can outweigh many short low-value intervals.

title: Merging intervals
summary: Sort intervals by start, then merge the next interval if it touches the current merged range. Sorting makes all future starts nondecreasing.
intuition: Sweep left to right, stretching the current covered segment until the next segment starts beyond its end.
clues: Union of covered ranges, calendar blocks, and overlapping segments. Endpoint conventions matter.
example: [2,6] begins before 3, so extend current to [1,6].
8 is beyond 6, so start a new segment: [[1,6],[8,10]].
state: Sorted intervals and the last merged interval.
invariant: Output intervals are sorted and disjoint, and their union equals the union of all processed intervals.
time: O(n log n) sorting plus O(n) scanning.
space: O(n) for sorted copy and output.
pitfalls: Replacing end instead of taking max can shrink a containing interval. Closed intervals merge on equality.
edges: Nested intervals, touching endpoints, empty input, duplicate ranges.
brute: Pairwise merging can cost O(n²) or worse with repeated rescanning. A sweep line handles counts of simultaneous intervals.
interview: I would sweep left to right, stretching the current covered segment until the next segment starts beyond its end. The key guarantee is: Output intervals are sorted and disjoint, and their union equals the union of all processed intervals.
followup: Why use max(current end, next end)?
simpler: Sweep left to right, stretching the current covered segment until the next segment starts beyond its end.

quiz.question: Why use max(current end, next end)?
options: The next interval might be contained inside the current one
quiz.explanation: Merging [1,10] with [2,3] must keep the endpoint 10.

title: Matrix rotation & coordinates
summary: Rotate a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise by transposing it and then reversing each row. Coordinate mapping explains the transformation.
intuition: Turn rows into columns, then flip each new row so the original top-left travels to the top-right.
clues: Square in-place rotation, coordinate transforms, and grid manipulation. Rectangular matrices need a differently shaped output.
state: Row and column indices; only swap entries above the main diagonal.
invariant: Transposition sends (r,c) to (c,r), then row reversal sends it to (c,n−1−r), the clockwise rotation mapping.
time: O(n²): every matrix cell is moved a constant number of times.
space: O(1) auxiliary space; mutates the input.
pitfalls: Swapping both halves transposes twice and cancels the change. This implementation requires a square matrix.
edges: Empty matrix, 1×1, repeated values, square shape required.
brute: Build a new matrix using rotated coordinates in O(n²) extra space.
interview: I would turn rows into columns, then flip each new row so the original top-left travels to the top-right. The key guarantee is: Transposition sends (r,c) to (c,r), then row reversal sends it to (c,n−1−r), the clockwise rotation mapping.
followup: Where does cell (r,c) move after a clockwise rotation?
simpler: Turn rows into columns, then flip each new row so the original top-left travels to the top-right.

quiz.question: Where does cell (r,c) move after a clockwise rotation?
quiz.explanation: Transposition followed by row reversal produces (c,n−1−r).

title: Bits & XOR cancellation
summary: XOR compares corresponding bits. Equal values cancel because x XOR x = 0, and x XOR 0 = x.
intuition: Pair up identical numbers. Every pair cancels out, leaving the unpaired value.
clues: Exactly one unpaired value when all others occur twice, parity, masks, and compact subset state.
example: Reorder XOR using associativity and commutativity.
state: A running XOR accumulator.
invariant: The accumulator is the XOR of every processed element. Pairs cancel regardless of their positions.
time: O(n) for fixed-width integers; Python big-integer operations scale with bit length.
pitfalls: Applying this when other values occur three times. Python integers are unbounded; 32-bit questions may need masking.
edges: Single element, zero, negatives, exact pairing assumption required.
brute: A frequency map costs O(n) additional storage and supports general multiplicities.
interview: I would pair up identical numbers. Every pair cancels out, leaving the unpaired value. The key guarantee is: The accumulator is the XOR of every processed element. Pairs cancel regardless of their positions.
followup: Will simple XOR isolate one value if every other value occurs three times?
simpler: Pair up identical numbers. Every pair cancels out, leaving the unpaired value.

quiz.question: Will simple XOR isolate one value if every other value occurs three times?
options: No, three equal values XOR to that value
Only if all values are positive
quiz.explanation: x XOR x XOR x = x, so triples do not cancel.

title: 0–1 BFS
summary: When every edge weight is 0 or 1, a deque can replace Dijkstra’s heap. Zero-cost improvements go to the front and one-cost improvements to the back.
intuition: A free move stays in the current wave; a paid move joins the next wave.
clues: Shortest paths with binary edge costs, such as minimum direction changes. Weights must be exactly 0 or 1.
example: Start (0,0). Push 1 to back and 2 to front.
state: Deque of (distance,node) snapshots and a distance array.
invariant: Deque entries are processed in nondecreasing candidate distance; zero and one weights preserve this order. Stale entries are skipped.
time: O(V + E) for binary weights.
space: O(V + E) with queued snapshots, excluding graph storage.
pitfalls: Using a visited-on-discovery set blocks improvements. Treating all nonzero weights as one is incorrect.
edges: Zero-weight cycles, disconnected vertices, parallel edges.
brute: Dijkstra also works but adds heap overhead. Ordinary BFS incorrectly treats a free edge as one unit.
interview: I would a free move stays in the current wave; a paid move joins the next wave. The key guarantee is: Deque entries are processed in nondecreasing candidate distance; zero and one weights preserve this order. Stale entries are skipped.
followup: Where should a zero-cost improvement enter the deque?
simpler: A free move stays in the current wave; a paid move joins the next wave.

quiz.question: Where should a zero-cost improvement enter the deque?
quiz.explanation: It belongs to the current distance layer, before paths costing one more.

title: Fenwick tree
summary: A Fenwick tree supports point additions and prefix sums in logarithmic time. Each cell represents a block whose size is its lowest set bit.
intuition: Keep overlapping subtotal boxes. Updating one number adjusts only the few boxes containing it.
clues: Repeated point updates and range-sum queries. For a static array, prefix sums are simpler.
example: tree uses 1-based indices; index 4 summarizes all four elements.
prefix(3) reads blocks ending at 3 and 2: 3 + 3 = 6.
A range sum is prefix(right) - prefix(left).
state: One-based tree array; i & -i gives the low bit.
invariant: tree[i] holds the sum of the block ending at i of length lowbit(i). Query blocks partition the requested prefix.
time: This simple build is O(n log n); each update and query is O(log n).
pitfalls: Passing index 0 to an internal one-based update without converting would never advance. Store deltas for updates, not replacement values.
edges: Empty range, full prefix, negative updates. External ranges are half-open.
brute: Prefix sums give O(1) static queries but O(n) updates. Segment trees support more general aggregates.
interview: I would keep overlapping subtotal boxes. Updating one number adjusts only the few boxes containing it. The key guarantee is: tree[i] holds the sum of the block ending at i of length lowbit(i). Query blocks partition the requested prefix.
followup: Why prefer plain prefix sums when there are no updates?
simpler: Keep overlapping subtotal boxes. Updating one number adjusts only the few boxes containing it.

quiz.question: Why prefer plain prefix sums when there are no updates?
options: O(1) queries after O(n) build, with simpler code
quiz.explanation: Use the simplest data structure matching the operations you actually need.
